SUPPORT FOR AN ADULT CHILD INCAPACITATED FROM EARNING A LIVING — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan Alex Lee · Morgan Casey Lee

DECLARATION OF PARTIES AND PURPOSE OF THIS INFORMATION SHEET
This Support for an Adult Child Incapacitated from Earning a Living Information Sheet concerns Jordan Alex Lee and Morgan Casey Lee, the parents of Casey Alex Lee, in connection with a proceeding pending, or that may be filed, in the California superior court for Sacramento County. It describes what California's Family Code says about a parent's duty of support toward a child who, regardless of the child's age, is incapacitated from earning a living and without sufficient means — a distinct statutory duty from the ordinary child-support obligation that applies to a minor child or to an unmarried child who has turned 18 and is still a full-time high school student. This information sheet states what the statute says in general terms. It does not determine, calculate, or assert that Casey Alex Lee is or is not incapacitated from earning a living within the meaning of that statute, that either parent owes or does not owe a support duty under it, or what amount of support (if any) would be appropriate; those are matters for the court to decide based on the specific facts, or for Jordan Alex Lee and Morgan Casey Lee to resolve by their own agreement.

THE STATUTORY DUTY — SUPPORT OF A CHILD INCAPACITATED FROM EARNING A LIVING
California's Family Code imposes on each parent of a child an equal responsibility, to the extent of that parent's ability, to maintain their child of whatever age who is incapacitated from earning a living and without sufficient means. This duty is not limited by the child's age; it applies regardless of whether the child has reached adulthood, so long as the child is both incapacitated from earning a living and lacks sufficient means of their own support.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "(a) Each parent of a child has an equal responsibility to maintain, to the extent of their ability, their child of whatever age who is incapacitated from earning a living and without sufficient means."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 3910(a) (California Legislative Information text), each parent's equal, ability-based duty to support a child of any age who is incapacitated from earning a living and without sufficient means (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=3910.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's own statutory support duty toward an incapacitated adult child — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific family, and not a claim that the child named in this document, or any other specific person, meets the statutory description. The statute does not itself define "incapacitated from earning a living" or "sufficient means," and this document does not supply definitions for those terms; a CourtListener case-law search for California appellate decisions construing this phrase, attempted during this research, returned a 429 rate-limit response (CourtListener's 125-request daily quota was exhausted) rather than usable results, so this clause rests on the statutory text alone and does not report on how courts have applied it in practice. The source's raw HTML places a non-breaking space (character U+00A0) between the subsection label "(a)" and the word "Each"; that non-breaking space is rendered as a regular space in the quote below, verified against the raw fetched HTML of both User-Agent fetches, which were textually identical.

HOW THIS DUTY RELATES TO THE ORDINARY DUTY TO SUPPORT A MINOR CHILD
The statute creating this incapacitated-adult-child support duty expressly states that it does not limit the separate, ordinary duty of a parent to support a minor child, or an unmarried child who has turned 18, is a full-time high school student, and is not self-supporting, until that child completes the 12th grade or turns 19. The two duties are independent statutory provisions that can apply to the same family at different times or in different circumstances; a family's ordinary minor-child support duty ending because a child has turned 19 or is no longer in high school does not by itself end any separate duty that may exist under the incapacitated-adult-child provision.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "(c) This section does not limit the duty of support under Sections 3900 and 3901."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 3910(c) (California Legislative Information text), the incapacitated-adult-child duty does not limit the separate minor/high-school-student support duty (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=3910.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence that California's own Family Code treats the incapacitated-adult-child support duty as a distinct provision layered on top of, not a substitute for, the ordinary minor/high-school-student support duty codified elsewhere in the same chapter (Family Code sections 3900 and 3901) — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific case. This document does not restate or re-verify the text of sections 3900 or 3901 themselves (already addressed elsewhere in this corpus); it verifies only this section's own cross-reference to them. The source's raw HTML inserts a line-break-and-tab artifact between the words "3900" and "and 3901" (the point where the official page's underlying paragraph markup wraps); that artifact is rendered as a single regular space in the quote below, verified against the raw fetched HTML of both User-Agent fetches, which were textually identical.

COURT'S OPTION TO DIRECT PAYMENT TO A SPECIAL NEEDS TRUST
California's Family Code gives the court an option, in a proceeding under this incapacitated-adult-child support provision, to order that a support payment be paid to a special needs trust rather than directly to the adult child or the child's other parent. The statute defines "special needs trust," for this purpose, by cross-reference to specific federal Medicaid-trust provisions and a specific California regulation governing trusts that do not count against certain public-benefit resource limits.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "(b) The court may order that a support payment be paid to a special needs trust. For purposes of this section, “special needs trust” means a trust that meets the requirements described in subparagraph (A) or (C) of paragraph (4) of subsection (d) of Section 1396p of Title 42 of the United States Code and paragraph (3) or (4) of subdivision (a) of Section 50489.9 of Title 22 of the California Code of Regulations."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 3910(b) (California Legislative Information text), the court's option to order a support payment paid to a special needs trust, and the statute's cross-referenced definition of that term (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=3910.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence that California law gives a family court this specific option — not a claim that a court will exercise it in any particular case, and not a claim about what other states' law provides. This document quotes the statute's own cross-reference to 42 U.S.C. section 1396p(d)(4)(A) and (C) and to California Code of Regulations, title 22, section 50489.9(a)(3) and (4), but this research did not independently fetch or verify the text of either the federal statute or the state regulation; readers should not assume this document has verified what those cross-referenced provisions themselves say, only that Family Code section 3910(b) cites them by this description. This document also does not address the separate body of law (addressed elsewhere in this corpus in an estate-planning context) governing how a special needs trust must be drafted or administered to preserve a beneficiary's eligibility for means-tested public benefits; it addresses only the family court's statutory option to direct a support payment into such a trust.

WHERE THIS DUTY SITS IN THE FAMILY CODE, AND ITS RECENT AMENDMENT
This support duty is codified in its own article of the Family Code — Article 2, "Support of Adult Child" — which today consists of this single section, within the chapter governing a parent's duty to support a child generally. The special-needs-trust payment option described in this document's companion clause is a comparatively recent addition to this section: the version of the statute in effect as of this research was last amended effective January 1, 2025.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "ARTICLE 2. Support of Adult Child [3910- 3910.]"
  — Cal. Fam. Code, Div. 9, Pt. 2, Ch. 1, Art. 2 heading (California Legislative Information text), this duty is codified as its own single-section article, titled "Support of Adult Child" (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=3910.)
  "(Amended by Stats. 2024, Ch. 25, Sec. 1. (AB 2397) Effective January 1, 2025.)"
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 3910, amendment history note (California Legislative Information text), the current text was last amended effective January 1, 2025 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=3910.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of where California places this duty within its own code structure and of when its current text took effect — not a claim about any other state's statutory organization. This research did not fetch or review the pre-amendment version of section 3910 (as it read before the 2024 amendment), so this document does not describe what the special-needs-trust option looked like, or whether it existed at all, before that amendment; it states only that the amendment identified in the quote below is the most recent one reflected on the official legislative information website as of the checked date. A CourtListener search was not separately attempted for this clause; the single CourtListener attempt made for this document's core-duty clause returned a 429 rate-limit response, so no case law confirming or discussing this amendment's legislative history was located or is relied on here.

EXPLANATORY NOTE — NO STATED MARITAL-STATUS CONDITION IN THIS PROVISION
This document's companion clause on the core statutory duty quotes the full text of the operative subsection. Readers comparing that text to the separate minor/high-school-student support provision (which by its own terms applies only to an "unmarried" child) may notice that the incapacitated-adult-child provision quoted in this document does not itself state an unmarried-child condition. This document does not interpret what that difference in wording means or does not mean for any specific family's circumstances; it only draws the reader's attention to it as a textual point worth discussing with a court or, where appropriate, a lawyer.

EXPLANATORY NOTE — RELATIONSHIP TO CALIFORNIA'S STATEWIDE CHILD SUPPORT GUIDELINE
California's statewide uniform guideline for calculating child support, addressed in this corpus's own guideline child-support and income-determination materials, is generally framed around the support of a minor child (or a child within the extended high-school-student period). This document does not restate that guideline formula, and it does not assert that the guideline formula does or does not apply, in whole or in part, to a support determination under the incapacitated-adult-child provision described in this document. Whether, and how, guideline principles inform a court's exercise of discretion under that separate provision is a legal question this document does not resolve.

EXPLANATORY NOTE — POSSIBLE INTERACTION WITH PUBLIC BENEFITS AND CONSERVATORSHIP
An adult child who is incapacitated from earning a living may, depending on individual circumstances, also be a recipient of means-tested public benefits, or may be subject to a probate conservatorship of the person or estate, or both. This document does not describe the rules governing eligibility for any public benefit program, and it does not describe the law governing conservatorship proceedings; those are each addressed, where this corpus addresses them, in separate materials. This document notes only that a support order or a special needs trust under the provision described in this document may need to be considered alongside those other, separate legal frameworks, without stating how any such consideration should come out in a particular family's situation.

INFORMATION COMMONLY GATHERED BEFORE RAISING THIS DUTY IN A PROCEEDING
Parties who wish to raise the incapacitated-adult-child support duty described in this document, whether by request to a court or by their own agreement, commonly gather information such as: Casey Alex Lee's current living situation and sources of income or support, if any; documentation bearing on the nature and duration of the incapacity; each parent's current ability to contribute to support, to the extent that is relevant; and, if a special needs trust is under discussion, the trust's name and any trustee already identified (The Casey Alex Lee Special Needs Trust). Gathering this information does not itself establish that the statutory duty applies; it is simply background information commonly assembled before the question is raised with a court or discussed between the parties.

SIGNATURE AND ACKNOWLEDGMENT — NOT A COURT FILING
I declare under penalty of perjury under the laws of the State of California that the foregoing background information is true and correct.

Executed on September 6, 2026 at Sacramento, California.
